tldr: The authors introduce "HumanoidVLN," a Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) simulator and benchmark that faithfully reproduces locomotion-induced camera dynamics, fall risks, and embodiment-specific physical constraints in humanoid robots, showing model behaviors under physics simulation and strong correlation with real-world hardware.
overview:
Research on Vision-Language Navigation (VLN)—guiding agents to destinations using visual inputs and language instructions—is growing rapidly. However, many existing simulators rely on "kinematic teleportation," where agents move instantaneously through space. While this might be acceptable for wheeled robots, bipedal humanoids face locomotion-induced camera shake, lighting variations, fall risks, and differences in center-of-mass dynamics caused by robot size and degrees of freedom (DoF), all of which directly dictate navigation success. Existing benchmarks have largely ignored these physical constraints.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "HumanoidVLN," a physics-grounded platform built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. By combining a reinforcement learning (RL) locomotion policy with interchangeable PD or model predictive control (MPC) path trackers in a hierarchical stack, it simulates the physical walking dynamics of four distinct humanoids. In addition, the authors constructed 87 scenes with over 100 square meters of navigable floor space using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and artist designs, along with a high-quality instruction dataset verified by LLM/VLM pipelines and humans using first-person walking video footage.

Evaluating four major VLN models zero-shot revealed that JanusVLN, which explicitly handles 3D spatial representations, achieved the highest success rate. Meanwhile, taller robots with fewer leg DoF experienced fall rates reaching 70%, underscoring how heavily physical constraints impact performance. Furthermore, a pilot experiment on a real Unitree G1 robot showed a remarkably strong correlation ($r=0.935$) in navigation errors between simulation and reality, confirming that this platform accurately reflects real-world behavior.
contributions: Built an extensible humanoid VLN simulation environment with a hierarchical control stack (RL + PD/MPC) accounting for whole-body bipedal physical constraints and embodiment diversity (heights 1.17–1.80 m, lower-body 10–12 DoF).
Constructed 87 high-quality Real2Sim environments combining artist designs and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), each offering over 100 square meters of navigable area necessary for humanoid locomotion.

Developed a dataset of 933 highly accurate instruction episodes across four styles, generated from realistic walking egocentric video using a multi-agent pipeline (MAA) combined with human-in-the-loop verification.

Cross-evaluated four representative VLN models across four humanoid embodiments under physical simulation, demonstrated the critical role of physical metrics like Fall Rate alongside standard success metrics, and validated strong sim-to-real correlation on hardware.

sections.heading: Why Do Humanoids Need a Dedicated VLN Simulator?
sections.summary: Humanoid VLN presents distinct challenges: locomotion dynamics, embodiment variations, and locomotion-induced camera shake. To resolve these, this paper introduces a physics-driven simulator, 3D environments filtered for navigability, and an instruction generation pipeline grounded in realistic egocentric observations.
sections.details:
With humanoid robotics and VLN technologies advancing in parallel, the sim-to-real gap remains a major hurdle to their integration. The authors highlight three critical gaps in existing research:

- Gap 1 (Lack of humanoid-aware physics simulation): Conventional VLN environments often rely on teleportation-based movement, ignoring the physical constraints of bipedal locomotion. Even recent Isaac Sim-based studies treat humanoids as just another robot type without accounting for embodiment-specific walking dynamics.
- Gap 2 (Scarcity of humanoid-navigable scenes): Standard environments such as Matterport3D are cramped and filled with obstacles that trip up bipedal humanoids. Bipedal locomotion demands open spaces with minimal clutter.
- Gap 3 (Lack of realistic egocentric observations and grounded instructions): Existing datasets feature ideal video footage with smooth horizontal camera motion. In contrast, real humanoids experience severe head-camera shake and rapid lighting shifts with every step. Additionally, automated annotations by VLMs often suffer from spatial hallucinations.

To overcome these issues, this study presents "HumanoidVLN," supporting four embodiments including the Unitree G1, Unitree H1, and two internal robots. With 87 large-scale environments and 933 evaluation episodes, it conducts comprehensive zero-shot evaluations under physics simulation.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Prior Embodied Navigation Benchmarks?
sections.summary: Traditional VLN environments like Habitat-Sim lack physical dynamics, and recent physics simulators have not addressed the bipedal locomotion constraints unique to humanoids. This work is the first benchmark to simultaneously tackle embodiment diversity, navigable space selection, and high-precision instruction generation.
sections.details:
Prior research in embodied navigation has evolved across two primary fronts: simulation platforms and task benchmarks.

- Simulation platforms: Habitat-Sim has long been the gold standard, but it relies on kinematic step movement and cannot simulate dynamic walking. While physics-engine-backed simulators such as VLN-PE and VLNVerse based on NVIDIA Isaac Sim have emerged, they treat humanoids as interchangeable with wheeled agents, stopping short of evaluating embodiment-specific locomotion policies or bipedal stability.
- 3D scene reconstruction: The advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has enabled photorealistic environment rendering. However, prior efforts like SAGE-3D did not filter scenes based on humanoid navigability and relied heavily on artist-created meshes.
- VLN benchmarks: Expanding from R2R and RxR into continuous environments (VLN-CE) and long-horizon tasks, benchmarks have largely left unexplored the influence of center-of-mass dynamics and gait stability on path tracking.

HumanoidVLN addresses these limitations comprehensively by integrating dedicated RL locomotion policies for each embodiment and automatically extracting high-quality collision meshes from 3DGS.

sections.heading: A Hierarchical Control Architecture for Diverse Humanoids
sections.summary: The platform supports four humanoids differing in height and lower-body degrees of freedom. Combining low-level RL locomotion policies with high-level path trackers (PD/MPC), it achieves physically executable navigation.
sections.details:
The core of the platform is a control system designed to faithfully simulate diverse humanoid morphologies (embodiment diversity).

- Supported embodiments: The platform supports four distinct humanoid robots spanning diverse builds and degrees of freedom: Unitree G1 (1.32 m, 12 lower-body DoF), Unitree H1 (1.80 m, 10 DoF), Internal-A (1.61 m), and Internal-B (1.17 m).
- Hierarchical control stack: The control system is organized into two layers. At the lower level, an RL locomotion policy trained for each specific embodiment directly commands joint torques, generating stable walking while respecting center-of-mass (CoM) dynamics and joint limits. At the higher level, a PD controller handles discrete actions, while a model predictive control (MPC) path tracker handles continuous actions, translating navigation headings and velocities output by VLN models into setpoints for the low-level policy.
- Unified interface and data recording: The platform records RGB, depth, and IMU data directly from the robot's head camera, complete with real walking shake. VLN models only need to accept head RGB images and text instructions and return actions, allowing seamless integration of models like NaVILA, DualVLN, StreamVLN, and JanusVLN without model-side modifications.

sections.heading: Reconstructing Expansive, Navigable Spaces with 3DGS
sections.summary: To provide adequate clearance for humanoid walking, the authors selected 87 scenes with over 100 square meters of navigable space. They established a dedicated Real2Sim pipeline that trains 3DGS on multi-view captures and extracts accurate meshes for physics collision.
sections.details:
Bipedal robots are prone to tripping and foot instability compared to wheeled agents, making them easily trapped by narrow doorways or small floor clutter. The environment pipeline incorporates specific innovations to address this:

- Filtering by navigable area: From 17 indoor environment categories spanning residential, retail, cultural, office, medical, and fitness domains, the authors selected only scenes where the collision mesh offers more than 100 square meters of walkable floor area. Across all 87 scenes, the median navigable area is 266 square meters, with an average of 387 square meters.
- 3DGS pipeline for precise collision meshes: Alongside artist-modeled scenes, the authors established a pipeline to construct photorealistic simulation environments directly from real-world multi-view images. Built upon the gsplat library, it incorporates unbiased depth rendering and depth-normal consistency, recovering clean, smooth surface normals along flat walls and furniture boundaries, and generating watertight collision meshes via TSDF fusion for seamless use in Isaac Sim.
- Physics-aware episode generation: The pipeline plans $A^*$ paths on 2D occupancy grids expanded by the robot's maximum turning radius, retaining only trajectories where the humanoid successfully and stably completes walking under the hierarchical control stack.

captions.F4: Comparison of surface normals in the 3DGS reconstruction pipeline. Standard gsplat produces noisy wall surfaces and furniture boundaries unsuitable for collision checking, whereas the full pipeline incorporating depth-normal consistency and unbiased depth (far right) recovers smooth, geometrically accurate surfaces.

sections.heading: Instruction Annotation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Human Review
sections.summary: Accurate instructions were generated from realistic first-person walking video by coordinating LLMs/VLMs assigned to generation, review, and paraphrasing roles. Human reviewers verified all samples, compiling 933 hallucination-free episodes.
sections.details:
Asking a single VLM to watch a video and output instructions often results in hallucinations, such as referencing non-existent landmarks or misidentifying turning directions. To counter this, this study designed a role-separated Multi-Agent Annotation (MAA) pipeline:

- Route generation agents: After identifying the target landmark from the final frame, two distinct models—Gemma-4-31B-it and InternVL3.5-38B—independently generate structured "route graphs" (capturing actions, landmarks, spatial relations, and turn angles) based solely on keyframes from the first-person walking video. Comparing structured graphs rather than raw text helps absorb stylistic variations.
- Cross-validation and review: The two route graphs are compared, and discrepancies are arbitrated by a reviewer agent (Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). During review, the agent queries a semantic scene graph containing only objects visible along the robot's actual trajectory, preventing the inclusion of landmarks the agent never actually saw.
- Style expansion and human verification: Based on the verified route, detailed instructions are paraphrased by GPT-5.5 into three distinct styles: formal, natural, and casual. Finally, three trained human annotators inspected and corrected every episode against the video footage, producing a verified evaluation set of 933 episodes.

sections.heading: What Physics Simulation and Real-Robot Trials Reveal About Humanoid VLN
sections.summary: Zero-shot evaluation of four leading VLN models showed that JanusVLN, equipped with 3D spatial awareness, achieved the top performance. Meanwhile, embodiment differences proved stark, with the Unitree H1 experiencing fall rates up to 71%, and real-world pilot tests demonstrated a strong correlation ($r=0.935$) with simulation results.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated four models—NaVILA, StreamVLN, DualVLN, and JanusVLN—zero-shot without fine-tuning. In addition to standard success rate (SR) and path fidelity (nDTW), the benchmark introduces Fall Rate (FR) to catch abrupt drops or collapses during walking.

- Cross-model performance (Q1): JanusVLN led the pack with a mean SR of 43.55% and mean nDTW of 48.38. Its explicit 3D spatial representation likely aided accurate localization and goal estimation despite camera shake. DualVLN, tracking continuous actions via MPC, also demonstrated strong trajectory fidelity (nDTW 43.39).
- Embodiment diversity and fall impact (Q2): Robot embodiments showed dramatic performance variations. Smaller, more stable platforms like Internal-A and the G1 kept fall rates between 2.7% and 10.0%, achieving SRs between 32% and 37%. In contrast, the tall (1.80 m) Unitree H1 with fewer leg DoF dropped to an average SR of 20.84%, with fall rates climbing to 64.5–71.0% under certain models. This shows that staying upright while walking is as critical to humanoid VLN as following instructions.
- 3DGS mesh quality (Q3): As illustrated in Fig. F4, the proposed 3DGS reconstruction pipeline yielded surface normals with minimal noise, validating its ability to produce workable collision meshes for physics simulation.
- Sim-to-real correlation (Q4): In a 20-episode real-world experiment pairing DualVLN with the Unitree G1 across a pantry and a studio, simulation and physical navigation errors showed a Pearson correlation coefficient of $r=0.935$. The mean absolute difference in final position error was only 0.68 m, demonstrating that the simulator reliably mirrors real-world behavior.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Directions
sections.summary: HumanoidVLN is the first humanoid VLN benchmark addressing physics dynamics, embodiment diversity, realistic scenes, and instruction accuracy. While navigating current challenges in scene scale and simulation overhead, future plans include incorporating 3D foundation models and broader hardware validation.
sections.details:
This paper presented "HumanoidVLN," a vision-language navigation environment that explicitly accounts for humanoid walking dynamics. Featuring a hierarchical control stack that absorbs diverse embodiment dynamics, 87 Real2Sim scenes with over 100 square meters of walkable space, and 933 hallucination-free instruction episodes, the platform demonstrates close alignment between physics simulation and real hardware.

Identified limitations include the bottleneck of human verification when scaling up datasets, along with the high computational cost of full-body physics simulation. The authors plan to integrate 3D foundation models for instruction grounding, develop more efficient 3DGS mesh reconstruction techniques, and conduct broader sim-to-real evaluations across additional hardware platforms.

takeaways: Teleportation assumptions do not hold for humanoid VLN; locomotion-induced camera shake and the risk of falling heavily dictate navigation success.
Differences in robot height and lower-body DoF can cause fall rates to swing from a few percent to over 70%, requiring embodiment-aware navigation strategies even within the exact same environment.
A 3DGS pipeline incorporating unbiased depth estimation and depth-normal consistency can automatically construct physics-ready collision environments from real-world scans without manual 3D modeling.
Navigation errors in simulation correlate strongly ($r=0.935$) with real-robot trials, proving that a physics-grounded Isaac Sim environment can reliably predict physical hardware performance.
limitations: Ensuring instruction quality across all episodes relies on manual verification by human annotators, creating a cost bottleneck for large-scale dataset expansion.
Simulating rigid-body dynamics and whole-body joint torque control incurs substantially higher computational overhead compared to traditional teleportation-based simulators.

Real-world sim-to-real validation is currently limited to a pilot study on a single robot model (Unitree G1) across two indoor scenes (20 episodes total), leaving broader generalization across diverse hardware and environments as future work.
